# Accessibility checklist

Reproducible output should also be usable output.

## Structure

- Use headings in order; do not choose levels for visual size.
- Use real lists and tables rather than spaces or manual line breaks.
- Give links descriptive text rather than “click here”.
- State the document language.

## Figures

Every meaningful figure should have `fig-alt` that describes:

- the chart type;
- the variables and comparison;
- the major visible pattern; and
- information not already supplied by the caption.

Do not begin with “image of”. Decorative images should have empty alt text.

## Colour

- Do not encode groups by colour alone; add shape, labels, or direct annotation
  where practical.
- Use palettes with adequate contrast.
- Check figures in greyscale.
- Avoid red/green as the only distinction.

## Tables and code

- Keep tables small and give them captions.
- Avoid merged cells where possible.
- Wrap long code lines and avoid screenshots of code.
- Explain what a code example is intended to demonstrate.

## Slides

- Use large text and high contrast.
- Keep one main idea per slide.
- Describe visual material aloud.
- Add speaker notes for required descriptions and facilitation cues.
- Provide the HTML or PDF afterward so participants can revisit the content.

## Final check

Inspect both HTML and PDF. A correct source does not guarantee equivalent
accessibility across output formats.
